title: How Squatting Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss squatting, starting with a detour into homelessness: the rise of homelessness after mental institutions closed, the expanded definition of homelessness, and the 2007 homeless count versus about 16.7 million vacant housing units. They cover groups doing homeless move-ins into vacant Miami houses (Take Back the Land) and the San Francisco Tenants Union. They define squatting as living on unused property that is not yours, distinguish it from home invasion, and explain squatters' protections: property and tenant rights (Georgia's three-day rule), and adverse possession (open, continuous, hostile occupation for a set period, varying by state, with property taxes paid). Chuck describes his own claim to a small strip of land behind his house in Georgia. They explain tactics like putting utilities in your name to shift the burden of proof, the legal difficulty for landlords evicting squatters (a story from CEO Mike Castcon), gentrification and developers as the squatter's main enemy (a squat torn down down the street; Geneva's Rhino group falling from 150 buildings to 27 by 2007), and Hernando de Soto's proposal to legalize squatters' land in post-Soviet countries, tried in Transnistria. The episode ends with a listener mail about a G. who described black ops stories relating to the Delta Force podcast.

segments.title: Intro and banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, with Josh introducing the topic of homelessness and the link to squatting.

segments.title: Homelessness, mental institutions and the homeless count
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the rise of homelessness after state mental institutions closed, a rumor about New York and Reagan-era shutdowns, the expanded definition of homelessness, and the 2007 homeless count versus vacant housing units.

segments.title: Homeless move-ins into vacant houses
segments.summary: Take Back the Land in Miami stages homeless move-ins into vacant bank-owned houses; the San Francisco Tenants Union and Home Not Jails are also mentioned; the hosts discuss housing as a human right.

segments.title: Defining squatting and squatter protections
segments.summary: Squatting is defined as living on unused property that is not yours, distinct from home invasion. Squatters have some protections: property and tenant rights, with Georgia's tenant rule kicking in after three days.

segments.title: Adverse possession
segments.summary: Adverse possession is explained as open, continuous, hostile occupation for a state-set period, with examples of time limits in California, West Virginia and Texas, and property taxes making the claim official.

segments.title: Chuck's squatting story
segments.summary: Chuck describes claiming a small strip of land behind his Georgia house that the previous owner abandoned with back taxes owed, and says he and his wife are pursuing adverse possession.

segments.title: Establishing residence and evicting squatters
segments.summary: Squatters can prove tenancy by setting up utility accounts in their name, shifting the burden of proof. Mike Castcon describes a costly squatter eviction he endured, and the hosts note landlords cannot cut power or water.

segments.title: Gentrification, developers and Geneva's Rhino group
segments.summary: Gentrification and developers are the squatter's main threat; a squatted house down the street was torn down. Geneva's Rhino squatter group fell from 150 buildings in the nineties to 27 by 2007. Hernando de Soto's proposal to title squatters' land is mentioned, tried in Transnistria.

segments.title: Listener mail about Delta Force black ops
segments.summary: A listener named G. shares a story about a friend's black ops experience in the Reagan-era drug war, including land mines and a cow.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close, giving the email address for listener mail and a sponsor line.
